title: Two lungs
hook: John Paul II said the Church must breathe with both lungs, East and West

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kyiv's baptism, a whole city in the Dnieper. Your line was baptized in the river. Did the water remind you of them? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

Take one slow breath, right now, and notice it. Both sides of your chest rise. You don't decide to use the left lung or the right one. They work together, or you work less well. A pope from Poland, John Paul the Second, reached for exactly this picture when he wrote about Christians of East and West, long apart, and about the Church they belong to. Not a ladder, not a building, not an army. A pair of lungs. Today, two lungs.
screen: `ONE SLOW BREATH.` → `BOTH SIDES RISE.` → `A POPE'S PICTURE.`

segments.voice: Across this block we've met the first Christians and the Fathers, and they came from both halves of the old world. Greek speakers like John Chrysostom and John of Damascus. Latin speakers like Augustine, Leo and Gregory. Monks in Egypt, on Athos and at Monte Cassino. For a long time they belonged to one Church, praying in different languages and styles. Next, the long separation. East and West drifted apart over language, politics and theology, and in the end broke communion with each other. That wound is still open. Catholics and Orthodox Christians share the sacraments and the apostles, but don't yet share one table. Then, the picture. Pope John Paul the Second wrote, in his letter on Christian unity, that the Church must breathe with her two lungs, East and West. He meant that the Eastern traditions, their icons, their chant, their long liturgies, their monks, aren't decoration on a Latin Church. They are half of its breathing. And inside the Catholic Church itself, Eastern Catholic Churches, like the Ukrainian Greek Catholics we met yesterday, already pray in the Eastern way in communion with Rome. Underneath it is an older picture still. In Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, God "breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul." Breath is a gift before it's an achievement. And unity, for John Paul, was something to pray for, not to force. His letter takes its name from Jesus's prayer in John's Gospel: "That they all may be one." The carry is the two halves he meant: east and west.
screen: `FATHERS FROM BOTH HALVES.` · `A WOUND STILL OPEN.` · `BREATHE WITH TWO LUNGS.` · `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` · then, large: `EAST AND WEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe deeply twice. Sit up a little. Put one hand on the left side of your chest and one on the right. Breathe in slowly, filling both sides, and let it go. Once more, deeper, and let it go. Then let your breath return to normal and rest your hands. As it moves, notice that both sides are working, without being asked. If you pray, you can hold the words from John, that they all may be one, and let them ride the breath. If not, simply rest in breathing. The bell holds the time.
Two lungs. John Paul the Second's picture of the Church breathing with both its traditions, East and West. Today's word.
Your line: east and west. Today, when you notice your breath, let both sides fill, and remember the half of the Church you know less well. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church includes both the Latin Church and Eastern Catholic Churches with their own liturgies, and Catholics pray for unity with the Orthodox, especially in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

fork.setup: you're a pope who wants the Church's East and West to come together. which picture do you choose?
options: a strong army with one general.
a ladder with the West on top.
fork.reveal: John Paul chose two lungs: neither one is the boss, and a body needs both to breathe fully.

original.note: Greek: breath — the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the breath of life in Genesis 2:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice image about getting along.
what it means: the Eastern and Western traditions are both the Church's own breathing, not a main part and an extra.
what a scholar hears: John Paul's 'two lungs', in Ut Unum Sint, set beside his hope for unity with the Orthodox.

notes: Ut Unum Sint 54: the Church must breathe with her two lungs. Paraphrased (Vatican translations are under copyright). Year not stated. John Paul used the image earlier too.
'Poland, a country that sits where the Latin West and the Christian East have long met' is narration; confirm or cut.

The East-West separation is not dated under the claims rule (no 1054). 'Don't yet share one table' summarizes that Catholics and Orthodox are not in full communion; confirm wording, since Catholic canon law permits some sacramental sharing in limited cases.
Recap of earlier block days (John Chrysostom, John of Damascus, Augustine, Leo, Gregory, desert monks, Athos, Monte Cassino) assumes those days teach them; confirm against the final scripts.
Original: πνοή in LXX Genesis 2:7 (πνοὴν ζωῆς). Pronunciation given in modern-leaning form; confirm.
Practice adds a short return to normal breathing so it fills the two-minute sit; confirm.
Editor: cut the uncited narration about Poland's place between East and West, and the time claim 'for centuries'.

Auditor: the narrator no longer states what John Paul 'also meant' (Ut Unum Sint 54 speaks of East and West with the Orthodox in view); the Eastern Catholic Churches are now described as a fact alongside it.
